title: Ezra

stories.title: 📜 Ezra 1
summaryBullets: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation throughout his kingdom and to put it in writing as follows: (1:1).
“This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah. (1:2).
Whoever among you belongs to His people, may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel; He is the God who is in Jerusalem. (1:3).
And let every survivor, wherever he lives, be assisted by the men of that region with silver, gold, goods, and livestock, along with a freewill offering for the house of God in Jerusalem.’” (1:4).
So the family heads of Judah and Benjamin, along with the priests and Levites— everyone whose spirit God had stirred— prepared to go up and rebuild the house of the LORD in Jerusalem. (1:5).
And all their neighbors supported them with articles of silver and gold, with goods and livestock, and with valuables, in addition to all their freewill offerings. (1:6).
King Cyrus also brought out the articles belonging to the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the temple of his gods. (1:7).
Cyrus king of Persia had them brought out by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah. (1:8).
This was the inventory: 30 gold dishes, 1,000 silver dishes, 29 silver utensils, (1:9).
30 gold bowls, 410 matching silver bowls, and 1,000 other articles. (1:10).
In all, there were 5,400 gold and silver articles. Sheshbazzar brought all these along when the exiles went up from Babylon to Jerusalem. (1:11).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 36:22-23: Chronicles ends with the same decree of Cyrus, in almost the same words.
Jeremiah 29:10-14: The LORD promises to bring the exiles back when seventy years are completed for Babylon.
Isaiah 44:24-28: The LORD calls Cyrus His shepherd, who will say of Jerusalem that it shall be built.
Isaiah 45:1-7: The LORD takes Cyrus by the right hand to open doors before him, though Cyrus does not know Him.
Daniel 5:1-4: Belshazzar drinks from the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar carried off from Jerusalem.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוֹרֶשׁ (Koresh) - Old Persian: Kurush - Greek: Κῦρος (Kyros)
translationNotes.note: Cyrus II, founder of the Persian empire. He took Babylon in 539 BC without a siege, and his first year as king of Babylon began in 538 BC, which is the year this decree is dated to. Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1 name him before he was born.

A clay barrel inscribed in Babylonian cuneiform, found in the ruins of Babylon in 1879 by Hormuzd Rassam and now in the British Museum. In it Cyrus states that he returned the gods of conquered cities to their sanctuaries and sent their people home to their settlements. Ezra 1:2-4 is that same imperial policy applied to Jerusalem, which had no image to return, only a house to rebuild.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּלֵי בֵית־יְהוָה (kelei beit YHWH, vessels of the house of the LORD)
translationNotes.note: Nebuchadnezzar stripped the temple in stages and carried the gold and silver service to Babylon (2 Kings 24:13; 25:14-15), and Belshazzar drank from it at his last feast (Daniel 5:2-3). Cyrus has Mithredath the treasurer count it back out by hand to Sheshbazzar: thirty gold basins, a thousand silver basins, thirty gold bowls, four hundred and ten silver bowls, and the rest, five thousand four hundred items in all. Returning captured cult property was standard Persian practice, and this is the inventory receipt.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁשְׁבַּצַּר (Sheshbatstsar)
translationNotes.note: Called 'the prince of Judah' (1:8), a Babylonian name of the kind given to exiles at court. He receives the vessels by count and is later described as the governor who laid the foundation of the house (5:14-16). The office he holds is pechah, the Persian-appointed governor of a province.

translationNotes.term: Silver, gold, goods and beasts from their neighbours
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְכָל־הַסְּבִיבֹתֵיהֶם חִזְּקוּ בִידֵיהֶם (vekhol hasevivotehem chizzequ videihem)
translationNotes.note: Ezra 1:4-6 has the people who stayed behind hand silver, gold, goods, livestock and freewill offerings to those going up. The wording deliberately matches Exodus 12:35-36, where Israel left Egypt carrying silver, gold and clothing given by their neighbours. The book reports the second exodus in the language of the first.

stories.keyTakeaway: Cyrus king of Persia issues a proclamation allowing the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple, with support from their neighbors; he also returns the temple articles that Nebuchadnezzar had taken, totaling 5,400 items of gold and silver that Sheshbazzar receives.

stories.title: 📜 Ezra 2
summaryBullets: Now these are the people of the province who came up from the captivity of the exiles carried away to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar its king. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town, (2:1).
accompanied by Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah. This is the count of the men of Israel: (2:2).
the descendants of Parosh, 2,172; (2:3).
the descendants of Shephatiah, 372; (2:4).
the descendants of Arah, 775; (2:5).
the descendants of Pahath-moab (through the line of Jeshua and Joab), 2,812; (2:6).
the descendants of Elam, 1,254; (2:7).
the descendants of Zattu, 945; (2:8).
the descendants of Zaccai, 760; (2:9).
the descendants of Bani, 642; (2:10).
the descendants of Bebai, 623; (2:11).
the descendants of Azgad, 1,222; (2:12).
the descendants of Adonikam, 666; (2:13).
the descendants of Bigvai, 2,056; (2:14).
the descendants of Adin, 454; (2:15).
the descendants of Ater (through Hezekiah), 98; (2:16).
the descendants of Bezai, 323; (2:17).
the descendants of Jorah, 112; (2:18).
the descendants of Hashum, 223; (2:19).
the descendants of Gibbar, 95; (2:20).
the men of Bethlehem, 123; (2:21).
the men of Netophah, 56; (2:22).
the men of Anathoth, 128; (2:23).
the descendants of Azmaveth, 42; (2:24).
the men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743; (2:25).
the men of Ramah and Geba, 621; (2:26).
the men of Michmash, 122; (2:27).
the men of Bethel and Ai, 223; (2:28).
the descendants of Nebo, 52; (2:29).
the descendants of Magbish, 156; (2:30).
the descendants of the other Elam, 1,254; (2:31).
the descendants of Harim, 320; (2:32).
the men of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 725; (2:33).
the men of Jericho, 345; (2:34).
and the descendants of Senaah, 3,630. (2:35).
The priests: The descendants of Jedaiah (through the house of Jeshua), 973; (2:36).
the descendants of Immer, 1,052; (2:37).
the descendants of Pashhur, 1,247; (2:38).
and the descendants of Harim, 1,017. (2:39).
The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel (through the line of Hodaviah), 74. (2:40).
The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 128. (2:41).

The gatekeepers: the descendants of Shallum, the descendants of Ater, the descendants of Talmon, the descendants of Akkub, the descendants of Hatita, and the descendants of Shobai, 139 in all. (2:42).
The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, the descendants of Hasupha, the descendants of Tabbaoth, (2:43).
the descendants of Keros, the descendants of Siaha, the descendants of Padon, (2:44).
the descendants of Lebanah, the descendants of Hagabah, the descendants of Akkub, (2:45).
the descendants of Hagab, the descendants of Shalmai, the descendants of Hanan, (2:46).
the descendants of Giddel, the descendants of Gahar, the descendants of Reaiah, (2:47).
the descendants of Rezin, the descendants of Nekoda, the descendants of Gazzam, (2:48).
the descendants of Uzza, the descendants of Paseah, the descendants of Besai, (2:49).
the descendants of Asnah, the descendants of Meunim, the descendants of Nephusim, (2:50).
the descendants of Bakbuk, the descendants of Hakupha, the descendants of Harhur, (2:51).
the descendants of Bazluth, the descendants of Mehida, the descendants of Harsha, (2:52).
the descendants of Barkos, the descendants of Sisera, the descendants of Temah, (2:53).
the descendants of Neziah, and the descendants of Hatipha. (2:54).
The descendants of the servants of Solomon: the descendants of Sotai, the descendants of Hassophereth, the descendants of Peruda, (2:55).
the descendants of Jaala, the descendants of Darkon, the descendants of Giddel, (2:56).
the descendants of Shephatiah, the descendants of Hattil, the descendants of Pochereth-hazzebaim, and the descendants of Ami. (2:57).
The temple servants and descendants of the servants of Solomon numbered 392 in all. (2:58).
The following came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, but they could not prove that their families were descended from Israel: (2:59).
the descendants of Delaiah, the descendants of Tobiah, and the descendants of Nekoda, 652 in all. (2:60).

And from among the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, the descendants of Hakkoz, and the descendants of Barzillai (who had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name). (2:61).
These men searched for their family records, but they could not find them and so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. (2:62).
The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim. (2:63).
The whole assembly numbered 42,360, (2:64).
in addition to their 7,337 menservants and maidservants, as well as their 200 male and female singers. (2:65).
They had 736 horses, 245 mules, (2:66).
435 camels, and 6,720 donkeys. (2:67).
When they arrived at the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, some of the heads of the families gave freewill offerings to rebuild the house of God on its original site. (2:68).
According to their ability, they gave to the treasury for this work 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priestly garments. (2:69).

So the priests, the Levites, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the temple servants, along with some of the people, settled in their own towns; and the rest of the Israelites settled in their towns. (2:70).
crossRefs: Nehemiah 7:6-73: The same register of returning families, copied into Nehemiah's account a century later.
1 Chronicles 9:1-3: The record of who came back and settled again in their own towns after the exile.
Exodus 28:29-30: The Urim and Thummim are placed in the fold of the high priest's breastpiece.
Numbers 3:5-10: The Levites are given to Aaron and his sons to do the work of the sanctuary.
Ezra 8:1-14: A second list, the heads of families who came up with Ezra a generation later.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִתְיַחֵשׂ (hityaches, to be enrolled by descent)
translationNotes.note: This chapter is a legal document, not a filler list. Land claims, tax liability and the right to serve at the altar all ran through recorded descent. Verses 59-63 name three priestly families who could not produce their record, and they were barred from eating the holy food until a priest should stand up with Urim and Thummim.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוּרִים וְתֻמִּים (Urim ve-Tummim)
translationNotes.note: Two objects kept in the fold of the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:30; Leviticus 8:8) and used to put a question to God that could be answered yes or no, or to single out one man from many (Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 14:41). By the return from exile no one was using them, which is why the disqualified priests in 2:63 were left waiting.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דַּרְכְּמוֹן (darkemon) and אֲדַרְכֹּן (adarkon)
translationNotes.note: The Persian gold coin, struck at about 8.4 grams of nearly pure gold (95.8 percent), a little over a quarter of a troy ounce. A soldier's pay was reckoned at one daric a month (Xenophon, Anabasis 1.3.21). The 61,000 darics given here come to roughly 512 kilograms, about 1,130 pounds, of gold.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָנֶה (maneh) - Greek: μνᾶ (mna)
translationNotes.note: A weight of silver, fifty shekels by the arithmetic behind Exodus 38:25-26, where a hundred talents equal three hundred thousand shekels; Ezekiel 45:12 reckons the maneh at sixty shekels. A shekel weighed about 11.4 grams, so a mina ran between roughly 570 and 685 grams, a little over a pound. The 5,000 minas here are on the order of three metric tons of silver.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְתִינִים (netinim, the given ones)
translationNotes.note: A hereditary class of temple labourers listed after the gatekeepers and singers, together with 'the sons of Solomon's servants'. Their work was the heavy end of sanctuary service: water, wood and hauling. Joshua 9:23-27 assigns exactly that duty to the Gibeonites for the altar of the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַתִּרְשָׁתָא (hattirshatha)
translationNotes.note: A Persian title for the governor of a province, used again of Nehemiah at Nehemiah 8:9 and 10:1. It is a loanword, not a Hebrew word, and it tells you the man giving the ruling in 2:63 held his authority from the Persian crown rather than from Israel's own law.

stories.keyTakeaway: The exiles return from Babylon to Jerusalem under leaders including Zerubbabel and Joshua, organized by family groups totaling 42,360 people plus servants and animals; upon arriving they contribute gold, silver, and priestly garments toward rebuilding the temple.

stories.title: 🏛️ Ezra 3
summaryBullets: By the seventh month, the Israelites had settled in their towns, and the people assembled as one man in Jerusalem. (3:1).

Then Jeshua son of Jozadak and his fellow priests, along with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his associates, began to build the altar of the God of Israel to sacrifice burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God. (3:2).
They set up the altar on its foundation and sacrificed burnt offerings on it to the LORD — both the morning and evening burnt offerings — even though they feared the people of the land. (3:3).
They also celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles in accordance with what is written, and they offered burnt offerings daily based on the number prescribed for each day. (3:4).
After that, they presented the regular burnt offerings and those for New Moons and for all the appointed sacred feasts of the LORD, as well as all the freewill offerings brought to the LORD. (3:5).
On the first day of the seventh month, the Israelites began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid. (3:6).

They gave money to the masons and carpenters, and food and drink and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring cedar logs from Lebanon to Joppa by sea, as authorized by Cyrus king of Persia. (3:7).

In the second month of the second year after they had arrived at the house of God in Jerusalem, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Jeshua son of Jozadak, and the rest of their associates including the priests, the Levites, and all who had returned to Jerusalem from the captivity, began the work. They appointed Levites twenty years of age or older to supervise the construction of the house of the LORD. (3:8).

So Jeshua and his sons and brothers, Kadmiel and his sons (descendants of Yehudah), and the sons of Henadad and their sons and brothers — all Levites — joined together to supervise those working on the house of God. (3:9).

When the builders had laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their apparel with trumpets, and the Levites (the sons of Asaph) with cymbals, took their positions to praise the LORD, as David king of Israel had prescribed. (3:10).

And they sang responsively with praise and thanksgiving to the LORD: “For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever.” Then all the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid. (3:11).
But many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple. Still, many others shouted joyfully. (3:12).
The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people were making so much noise. And the sound was heard from afar. (3:13).
crossRefs: Leviticus 23:33-43: The Feast of Booths is commanded for the fifteenth day of the seventh month, seven days in shelters.
Numbers 29:12-38: The daily burnt offerings prescribed for the eight days of Booths, thirteen bulls on the first day down to seven on the seventh.
1 Kings 5:6-11: Solomon buys cedar from Lebanon, paying Hiram in wheat and oil, the timber floated down the coast.
Haggai 2:1-9: The prophet asks who is left that saw the first house in its glory, and promises this house will be filled with glory.
Zechariah 4:8-10: The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundation and will finish it; do not despise the day of small things.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach, altar)
translationNotes.note: They build the altar on its old site and start the twice-daily burnt offering (Exodus 29:38-42; Numbers 28:3-8) in the seventh month, before a single stone of the house is laid. Exodus 20:24-25 requires an altar of earth or of uncut stone, so it could be built fast and by anyone. Sacrifice resumed roughly seven months before construction began.

translationNotes.term: Cedar from Lebanon by sea to Joppa
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶרֶז מִן־הַלְּבָנוֹן (erez min ha-Levanon)
translationNotes.note: Verse 7 pays the men of Sidon and Tyre in food, drink and oil for cedar logs floated down the coast to Joppa, the nearest port to Jerusalem, about thirty-five miles west and then a hard climb inland. This is the identical arrangement Solomon made for the first temple (1 Kings 5:6-11; 2 Chronicles 2:16). Lebanese cedar was the prestige structural timber of the region, rot-resistant and available in long straight lengths.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זְרֻבָּבֶל (Zerubbavel) - יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua)
translationNotes.note: Two offices, not two names for the same job. Zerubbabel is a grandson of King Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:17-19), so the royal line stands over the civil work; his name means 'seed of Babylon', where he was born. Jeshua son of Jozadak is the high priest, and his father was carried into exile when the first temple fell (1 Chronicles 6:15). Jeshua is the same name that Greek writes as Iesous.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַזְּקֵנִים אֲשֶׁר רָאוּ אֶת־הַבַּיִת הָרִאשׁוֹן (hazzeqenim asher ra'u et habbayit harishon)
translationNotes.note: Solomon's temple burned in 586 BC and this foundation is laid about 536 BC. Anyone who could remember the first house standing was past sixty, and they were weeping over a footprint far smaller than the one they had seen. The shout of the young men and the crying of the old carried the same distance and no one outside could tell them apart (3:12-13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲצֹצְרוֹת (chatsotserot, trumpets) - מְצִלְתַּיִם (metsiltayim, cymbals)
translationNotes.note: The trumpets are the priests' straight silver instruments commanded in Numbers 10:1-10, sounded for assembly, for war and over the offerings. The cymbals belong to the Levites under the order David set for the singers (1 Chronicles 15:16, 19). The music at the foundation is the old temple liturgy restarted from the books, not improvised.

stories.keyTakeaway: The returned exiles rebuild the altar under Joshua and Zerubbabel, restore the regular sacrifices and festivals, and lay the foundation of the temple with celebration; some older priests weep at the sight while others shout for joy.

stories.title: 🏛️ Ezra 4
summaryBullets: When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the exiles were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel, (4:1).

they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of the families, saying, “Let us build with you because, like you, we seek your God and have been sacrificing to Him since the time of King Esar-haddon of Assyria, who brought us here.” (4:2).

But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the other heads of the families of Israel replied, “You have no part with us in building a house for our God, since we alone must build it for the LORD, the God of Israel, as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us.” (4:3).
Then the people of the land set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build. (4:4).
They hired counselors against them to frustrate their plans throughout the reign of Cyrus king of Persia and down to the reign of Darius king of Persia. (4:5).
At the beginning of the reign of Xerxes, an accusation was lodged against the people of Judah and Jerusalem. (4:6).
And in the days of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of his associates wrote a letter to Artaxerxes. It was written in Aramaic and then translated. (4:7).
Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote the letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes as follows: (4:8).
From Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates— the judges and officials over Tripolis, Persia, Erech and Babylon, the Elamites of Susa, (4:9).
and the rest of the peoples whom the great and honorable Ashurbanipal deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and elsewhere west of the Euphrates. (4:10).
(This is the text of the letter they sent to him.) To King Artaxerxes, From your servants, the men west of the Euphrates: (4:11).

Let it be known to the king that the Jews who came from you to us have returned to Jerusalem and are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are restoring its walls and repairing its foundations. (4:12).
Let it now be known to the king that if that city is rebuilt and its walls are restored, they will not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury will suffer. (4:13).
Now because we are in the service of the palace and it is not fitting for us to allow the king to be dishonored, we have sent to inform the king (4:14).

that a search should be made of the record books of your fathers. In these books you will discover and verify that the city is a rebellious city, harmful to kings and provinces, inciting sedition from ancient times. That is why this city was destroyed. (4:15).
We advise the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are restored, you will have no dominion west of the Euphrates. (4:16).
Then the king sent this reply: To Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of your associates living in Samaria and elsewhere in the region west of the Euphrates: Greetings. (4:17).
The letter you sent us has been translated and read in my presence. (4:18).
I issued a decree, and a search was conducted. It was discovered that this city has revolted against kings from ancient times, engaging in rebellion and sedition. (4:19).
And mighty kings have ruled over Jerusalem and exercised authority over the whole region west of the Euphrates; and tribute, duty, and toll were paid to them. (4:20).
Now, therefore, issue an order for these men to stop, so that this city will not be rebuilt until I so order. (4:21).
See that you do not neglect this matter. Why allow this threat to increase and the royal interests to suffer? (4:22).
When the text of the letter from King Artaxerxes was read to Rehum, Shimshai the scribe, and their associates, they went immediately to the Jews in Jerusalem and forcibly stopped them. (4:23).
Thus the construction of the house of God in Jerusalem ceased, and it remained at a standstill until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia. (4:24).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 17:24-34: Assyria settles men from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim in the towns of Samaria, where they fear the LORD and serve their own gods.
Nehemiah 4:1-9: Sanballat and Tobiah jeer at the wall and then conspire to attack it.
Daniel 6:4-9: Officials who can find no fault in a man engineer a written royal decree that traps him.
Esther 3:8-11: A minister persuades a Persian king by charging that one people keeps laws unlike the king's laws.
Ezra 6:1-5: Darius orders the archives searched, and the scroll of Cyrus is found at Ecbatana.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: אֲרָמִית (aramit) - Hebrew: עִבְרִית (ivrit)
translationNotes.note: From 4:8 to 6:18, and again at 7:12-26, Ezra is written in Aramaic instead of Hebrew. Aramaic was the working language of Persian government from Egypt to India, so the letters, decrees and court records are quoted in the language they were actually filed in, while the narrative around them stays in Hebrew. The other Aramaic in Scripture is Daniel 2:4b-7:28, Jeremiah 10:11, and two words in Genesis 31:47.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: עֲבַר נַהֲרָה (avar naharah) - Hebrew: עֵבֶר הַנָּהָר (ever hannahar)
translationNotes.note: The Persian satrapy west of the Euphrates, taking in Syria, Phoenicia, Cyprus and the whole land bridge down to the Egyptian frontier. The name is written from the imperial capital looking west, so 'beyond the river' means beyond the Euphrates. Judah, called Yehud, was one small province inside it, and every letter in this chapter travels up and down that chain of command.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: בְּעֵל־טְעֵם (be'el te'em, commanding officer) - סָפְרָא (safra, scribe)
translationNotes.note: These are job titles, not honorifics. Be'el te'em is the provincial officer responsible for reports and decrees, and the safra is the secretary who drafted and filed the correspondence. The complaint against Jerusalem goes forward through the ordinary provincial paperwork, correctly formatted and correctly addressed.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: מִנְדָּה בְלוֹ וַהֲלָךְ (mindah, belo, va-halakh)
translationNotes.note: Three separate Persian revenue streams, named again at 4:20 and 7:24. Mindah is the assessed tribute of a province, belo is a levy in kind or produce, halakh is a toll on goods in transit. The accusation in 4:13 is not religious; it is that a walled Jerusalem will stop paying all three.

translationNotes.term: The kings in this chapter are out of order
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 names Ahasuerus (Xerxes, 486-465 BC) and verses 7-23 name Artaxerxes (465-424 BC), both of whom reigned after Darius, and then 4:24 picks the story back up in the reign of Darius (522-486 BC). The chapter gathers the whole file of opposition letters in one place before returning to the sequence of events. Read it as a dossier dropped into the narrative, not as a calendar.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)
translationNotes.note: The hill country north of Judah and the capital of the northern kingdom from about 880 BC until Assyria took it in 722 BC and deported the population. The men who offer to help build in 4:2 are descended from the settlers Assyria moved in afterwards, which is why they can say they have sacrificed to the God of Israel since Esarhaddon brought them up. The refusal in 4:3 is the beginning of the split that hardens into the Samaritan quarrel of the Gospels.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enemies of Judah and Benjamin offer to help build the temple and are refused; they discourage the builders, hire counselors against them, and write letters to Persian kings accusing Jerusalem of rebellion, until Artaxerxes orders the work stopped by force and construction ceases until the second year of Darius.

stories.title: 🏛️ Ezra 5
summaryBullets: Later, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, who was over them. (5:1).
Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. And the prophets of God were with them, helping them. (5:2).

At that time Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates went to the Jews and asked, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?” (5:3).
They also asked, “What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?” (5:4).
But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, so that they were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned. (5:5).
This is the text of the letter that Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates, the officials in the region, sent to King Darius. (5:6).
The report they sent him read as follows: To King Darius: All peace. (5:7).

Let it be known to the king that we went into the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. The people are rebuilding it with large stones and placing timbers in the walls. This work is being carried out diligently and is prospering in their hands. (5:8).
So we questioned the elders and asked, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?” (5:9).
We also asked for their names, so that we could write down the names of their leaders for your information. (5:10).

And this is the answer they returned: “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the temple that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and completed. (5:11).

But since our fathers angered the God of heaven, He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean who destroyed this temple and carried away the people to Babylon. (5:12).
In the first year of his reign, however, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this house of God. (5:13).

He also removed from the temple of Babylon the gold and silver articles belonging to the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken and carried there from the temple in Jerusalem. King Cyrus gave these articles to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor (5:14).
and instructed, ‘Take these articles, put them in the temple in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its original site.’ (5:15).
So this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been under construction, but it has not yet been completed.” (5:16).

Now, therefore, if it pleases the king, let a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon to see if King Cyrus did indeed issue a decree to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. Then let the king send us his decision in this matter. (5:17).
crossRefs: Haggai 1:1-15: In the second year of Darius the prophet rebukes the delay, and the people begin work on the house within a month.
Zechariah 1:1-6: Zechariah's first word comes two months after Haggai's, in the eighth month of the same year.
Ezra 1:1-4: The original decree of Cyrus that the elders cite to the Persian investigators.
2 Kings 25:8-12: Nebuchadnezzar burns the temple and the palace and deports the people, the event the elders summarise in their answer.
Ezra 4:1-5: The same neighbours had already hired counsellors to frustrate the building.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: תַּתְּנַי (Tattenai)
translationNotes.note: The Persian governor of Beyond the River, named four times in this book (5:3, 6; 6:6, 13). He is attested outside Scripture: a Babylonian promissory note dated to the twentieth year of Darius I, 502 BC, identifies a witness as the servant of 'Tattannu, governor of Across-the-River'. He is not an enemy in this chapter; he is an official checking a building permit.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: מַן־שָׂם לְכֹם טְעֵם (man sam lekhom te'em, who issued you a decree)
translationNotes.note: Tattenai does not stop the work. He records the names of the builders, takes their answer, and writes to the king asking that the treasury records be searched (5:9-17). Persian administration kept dated files, and the whole crisis is settled in chapter 6 by finding the right document. This is bureaucracy working in Judah's favour.

translationNotes.term: Great stones and timber in the walls
translationNotes.original: Aramaic: אֶבֶן גְּלָל וְאָע (even gelal ve-a', dressed stone and timber)
translationNotes.note: Verse 8 describes courses of large dressed stone with wooden beams laid into the wall between them. Solomon's temple was built the same way, three courses of cut stone to one course of cedar beams (1 Kings 6:36; 7:12). The timber ties the masonry together and gives it some give, which matters in earthquake country.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: פֶּחָה (pechah, governor)
translationNotes.note: In their letter the elders trace the legal chain: Cyrus took the vessels out of the temple of Babylon, handed them by name to a man he had appointed governor, and told him to put them back in Jerusalem (5:14-16). The point of naming him is that the permission is on file with a named officer of the crown, dated to a named king.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא (elah shemayya) - Hebrew: אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם (elohei hashamayim)
translationNotes.note: This is how Judeans name the LORD in Persian-period official documents, and it runs through Ezra, Nehemiah and Daniel (Ezra 1:2; 6:9-10; 7:12; Nehemiah 1:4; Daniel 2:18). It is a title a Persian court would recognise and file. In their own worship the name used is the LORD, the God of Israel (5:1).

stories.keyTakeaway: Haggai and Zechariah encourage Zerubbabel and Joshua to rebuild the temple; when Persian officials question their authority, the Jewish elders explain they are obeying Cyrus's original decree and request that King Darius verify this in the royal archives.

stories.title: 🏛️ Ezra 6
summaryBullets: Thus King Darius ordered a search of the archives stored in the treasury of Babylon. (6:1).
And a scroll was found in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media, with the following written on it: Memorandum: (6:2).

In the first year of King Cyrus, he issued a decree concerning the house of God in Jerusalem: Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices, and let its foundations be firmly laid. It is to be sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide, (6:3).
with three layers of cut stones and one of timbers. The costs are to be paid from the royal treasury. (6:4).

Furthermore, the gold and silver articles of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem and carried to Babylon, must also be returned to the temple in Jerusalem and deposited in the house of God. (6:5).
Therefore Darius decreed: To Tattenai governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and your associates and officials in the region: You must stay away from that place! (6:6).
Leave this work on the house of God alone. Let the governor and elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its original site. (6:7).

I hereby decree what you must do for these elders of the Jews who are rebuilding this house of God: The cost is to be paid in full to these men from the royal treasury out of the taxes of the provinces west of the Euphrates, so that the work will not be hindered. (6:8).

Whatever is needed— young bulls, rams, and lambs for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, as well as wheat, salt, wine, and oil, as requested by the priests in Jerusalem— must be given to them daily without fail. (6:9).
Then they will be able to offer sacrifices of a sweet aroma to the God of heaven and to pray for the lives of the king and his sons. (6:10).

I also decree that if any man interferes with this directive, a beam is to be torn from his house and raised up, and he is to be impaled on it. And his own house shall be made a pile of rubble for this offense. (6:11).

May God, who has caused His Name to dwell there, overthrow any king or people who lifts a hand to alter this decree or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have issued the decree. Let it be carried out with diligence. (6:12).
In response, Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates diligently carried out what King Darius had decreed. (6:13).

So the Jewish elders built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo. They finished building according to the command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, kings of Persia. (6:14).
And this temple was completed on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius. (6:15).
Then the people of Israel — the priests, the Levites, and the rest of the exiles — celebrated the dedication of the house of God with joy. (6:16).

For the dedication of the house of God they offered a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and a sin offering for all Israel of twelve male goats, one for each tribe of Israel. (6:17).
They also appointed the priests by their divisions and the Levites by their groups to the service of God in Jerusalem, according to what is written in the Book of Moses. (6:18).
On the fourteenth day of the first month, the exiles kept the Passover. (6:19).

All the priests and Levites had purified themselves and were ceremonially clean. And the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their priestly brothers, and for themselves. (6:20).
The Israelites who had returned from exile ate it, together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel. (6:21).

For seven days they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread with joy, because the LORD had made them joyful and turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them to strengthen their hands in the work on the house of the God of Israel. (6:22).
crossRefs: Esther 6:1-3: A Persian king has the book of records read to him at night, and an old entry changes everything.
2 Chronicles 7:4-10: Solomon's dedication of the first house, with sacrifices and a feast that ran fourteen days.
Exodus 12:1-20: The Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the first month, and seven days of unleavened bread after it.
2 Chronicles 30:13-22: Hezekiah keeps a Passover for a people who are not all ritually clean, and prays for them.
Zechariah 8:9-13: Let your hands be strong, you who hear these words from the prophets since the day the foundation was laid.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: אַחְמְתָא (Achmeta) - Old Persian: Hagmatana
translationNotes.note: The old Median capital, high in the Zagros mountains at about 6,000 feet, now the city of Hamadan in western Iran. The Persian court moved with the seasons, wintering at Babylon or Susa and summering in the cool of Ecbatana, and the records moved with it. The scroll of Cyrus was not in Babylon because Cyrus was not in Babylon when he issued it.

translationNotes.term: Impaled on a beam from his own house
translationNotes.original: Aramaic: יִזְקֵף עֲלֹהִי (yizqef alohi, he shall be lifted up on it)
translationNotes.note: The penalty in 6:11 is that a beam is torn out of the offender's house and he is fastened on it, and his house made a dunghill. This is impalement, the standard Persian punishment for defying a royal order; Darius records impaling rebel leaders in his own Behistun inscription. It is the same death, and the same Hebrew and Aramaic vocabulary of wood and lifting up, that stands behind the 'gallows' of Esther 5:14.

translationNotes.term: The house finished in the sixth year of Darius
translationNotes.original: Aramaic: יוֹם תְּלָתָה לִירַח אֲדָר (yom telatah lirach Adar, the third day of the month Adar)
translationNotes.note: Adar is the twelfth month, so the temple was completed in late winter, early in 515 BC. The first house had burned in 586 BC. Seventy-one years separate the fire from the finished replacement, which is why the exile is remembered in round numbers as seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲנֻכַּת בֵּית־אֱלָהָא (chanukkat beit elaha, dedication of the house of God)
translationNotes.note: A hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering, one for each tribe of Israel (6:17). Set that beside Solomon's dedication of the first house, twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep (1 Kings 8:63), and you can measure how small and how poor the returned community was. The twelve goats say they still counted themselves as all Israel, not just Judah and Benjamin.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר (melekh Ashur)
translationNotes.note: Verse 22 says the LORD turned the heart of 'the king of Assyria' toward them, and the king in question is Darius the Persian. Assyria had fallen in 612 BC. The title stuck to whoever held the old Assyrian lands, the way people kept saying 'the Great King' long after the dynasty changed. It is not an error and it is not a different king.

stories.keyTakeaway: King Darius finds Cyrus's original decree authorizing the temple's rebuilding, issues his own order supporting the work and threatening severe punishment for interference, and the Jewish elders complete the temple with Persian backing. The people dedicate the finished temple with sacrifices and celebrate Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread.

headings.text: The Returned Exiles Keep the Passover

stories.title: 📖 Ezra 7
summaryBullets: Many years later, during the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra son of Seraiah, the son of Azariah, the son of Hilkiah, (7:1).
the son of Shallum, the son of Zadok, the son of Ahitub, (7:2).
the son of Amariah, the son of Azariah, the son of Meraioth, (7:3).
the son of Zerahiah, the son of Uzzi, the son of Bukki, (7:4).
the son of Abishua, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the chief priest— (7:5).

this Ezra came up from Babylon. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses, which the LORD, the God of Israel, had given. The king had granted Ezra all his requests, for the hand of the LORD his God was upon him. (7:6).
So in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes, he went up to Jerusalem with some of the Israelites, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants. (7:7).
Ezra arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the seventh year of the king. (7:8).
He had begun the journey from Babylon on the first day of the first month, and he arrived in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month, for the gracious hand of his God was upon him. (7:9).
For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel. (7:10).
This is the text of the letter King Artaxerxes had given to Ezra the priest and scribe, an expert in the commandments and statutes of the LORD to Israel: (7:11).
Artaxerxes, king of kings. To Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven: Greetings. (7:12).
I hereby decree that any volunteers among the Israelites in my kingdom, including the priests and Levites, may go up with you to Jerusalem. (7:13).
You are sent by the king and his seven counselors to evaluate Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand. (7:14).
Moreover, you are to take with you the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem, (7:15).
together with all the silver and gold you may find in all the province of Babylon, as well as the freewill offerings of the people and priests to the house of their God in Jerusalem. (7:16).

With this money, therefore, you are to buy as many bulls, rams, and lambs as needed, together with their grain offerings and drink offerings, and offer them on the altar at the house of your God in Jerusalem. (7:17).
You and your brothers may do whatever seems best with the rest of the silver and gold, according to the will of your God. (7:18).
You must deliver to the God of Jerusalem all the articles given to you for the service of the house of your God. (7:19).
And if anything else is needed for the house of your God that you may have occasion to supply, you may pay for it from the royal treasury. (7:20).
I, King Artaxerxes, decree to all the treasurers west of the Euphrates: Whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven, may require of you, it must be provided promptly, (7:21).
up to a hundred talents of silver, a hundred cors of wheat, a hundred baths of wine, a hundred baths of olive oil, and salt without limit. (7:22).
Whatever is commanded by the God of heaven must be done diligently for His house. For why should wrath fall on the realm of the king and his sons? (7:23).
And be advised that you have no authority to impose tribute, duty, or toll on any of the priests, Levites, singers, doorkeepers, temple servants, or other servants of this house of God. (7:24).

And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God, which you possess, are to appoint magistrates and judges to judge all the people west of the Euphrates — all who know the laws of your God. And you are to teach these laws to anyone who does not know them. (7:25).
If anyone does not keep the law of your God and the law of the king, let a strict judgment be executed against him, whether death, banishment, confiscation of property, or imprisonment. (7:26).
Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who has put into the heart of the king to so honor the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, (7:27).

and who has shown me favor before the king, his counselors, and all his powerful officials. And because the hand of the LORD my God was upon me, I took courage and gathered the leaders of Israel to return with me. (7:28).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 6:3-15: The full high-priestly line from Aaron down to the exile, which Ezra's genealogy abbreviates.
2 Kings 25:18-21: Seraiah the chief priest, Ezra's ancestor, is taken at Jerusalem and executed at Riblah.
Deuteronomy 16:18-20: Judges and officers are to be appointed in all your towns to judge the people with righteous judgment.
Deuteronomy 33:8-10: Levi's charge is to teach Jacob God's rules and Israel His law, and to keep the Urim and Thummim.
Malachi 2:4-7: The lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and men should seek instruction from his mouth.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֹפֵר (sofer) - Aramaic: סָפְרָא (safra) - Greek: γραμματεύς (grammateus)
translationNotes.note: The root means to count and to write, and in Persian service a sofer was a state secretary with a portfolio. Artaxerxes' letter titles Ezra 'the scribe of the law of the God of heaven' (7:12, 21), which reads as an imperial appointment: this man is the crown's authority on Jewish law inside the province. Verse 6 adds the other half of it, that he was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses.

translationNotes.term: The law of your God which is in your hand
translationNotes.original: Aramaic: דָּת אֱלָהָךְ דִּי בִידָךְ (dat elahakh di vidakh)
translationNotes.note: Dat is the Persian word for royal law, and the letter uses it for the Law of Moses. Ezra is empowered to appoint magistrates and judges for everyone in Beyond the River who knows the laws of his God, to teach those who do not, and to enforce judgment (7:25-26). The Persian crown is underwriting Israel's own law as provincial law.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: לְמוֹת אוֹ לִשְׁרֹשִׁי לַעֲנָשׁ נִכְסִין וְלֶאֱסוּרִין (limot o lishroshi la'anash nikhsin vele'esurin)
translationNotes.note: The sentence in 7:26 lists them in order: death, banishment, confiscation of goods, imprisonment. The second one literally means 'uprooting', being torn out of your place and sent away. This is the coercive power a Persian king delegated with a commission, spelled out in the document itself.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּכָּר (kikkar) - Greek: τάλαντον (talanton)
translationNotes.note: The largest weight in the ancient world, about 75 pounds or 34 kilograms, reckoned at 3,000 shekels. As money a talent of silver ran to roughly 6,000 denarii, and a denarius was a day's wage for a labourer (Matthew 20:2), so one talent is about twenty years of work. The hundred talents of silver granted in 7:22 come to about 3.4 metric tons.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּר (kor) - Greek: κόρος (koros)
translationNotes.note: The largest dry measure, about 220 litres or 58 gallons, equal to ten ephahs. The hundred kors of wheat in 7:22 amount to roughly 22,000 litres of grain, several tons of flour once milled. The steward in Luke 16:7 discounts a debt of a hundred kors of wheat, which is the same quantity.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּת (bath)
translationNotes.note: The liquid equivalent of the ephah, about 22 litres or 5.8 gallons. A hundred baths of wine and a hundred of oil (7:22) is around 2,200 litres of each, enough to keep the daily offerings running for a long time. For scale, the bronze sea in Solomon's temple held two thousand baths (1 Kings 7:26).

stories.keyTakeaway: Ezra, a priest and skilled teacher of the Law descended from Aaron, travels from Babylon to Jerusalem with royal permission and funding from King Artaxerxes, who grants him authority to enforce God's law and appoint judges throughout the region.

stories.title: 📖 Ezra 8
summaryBullets: These are the family heads and genealogical records of those who returned with me from Babylon during the reign of King Artaxerxes: (8:1).
from the descendants of Phinehas, Gershom; from the descendants of Ithamar, Daniel; from the descendants of David, Hattush (8:2).
of the descendants of Shecaniah; from the descendants of Parosh, Zechariah, and with him were registered 150 men; (8:3).
from the descendants of Pahath-Moab, Eliehoenai son of Zerahiah, and with him 200 men; (8:4).
from the descendants of Zattu, Shecaniah son of Jahaziel, and with him 300 men; (8:5).
from the descendants of Adin, Ebed son of Jonathan, and with him 50 men; (8:6).
from the descendants of Elam, Jeshaiah son of Athaliah, and with him 70 men; (8:7).
from the descendants of Shephatiah, Zebadiah son of Michael, and with him 80 men; (8:8).
from the descendants of Joab, Obadiah son of Jehiel, and with him 218 men; (8:9).
from the descendants of Bani, Shelomith son of Josiphiah, and with him 160 men; (8:10).
from the descendants of Bebai, Zechariah son of Bebai, and with him 28 men; (8:11).
from the descendants of Azgad, Johanan son of Hakkatan, and with him 110 men; (8:12).
from the later descendants of Adonikam, these were their names: Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah, and with them 60 men; (8:13).
and from the descendants of Bigvai, both Uthai and Zaccur, and with them 70 men. (8:14).
Now I assembled these exiles at the canal that flows to Ahava, and we camped there three days. And when I searched among the people and priests, I found no Levites there. (8:15).
Then I summoned the leaders: Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, as well as the teachers Joiarib and Elnathan. (8:16).
And I sent them to Iddo, the leader at Casiphia, with a message for him and his kinsmen, the temple servants at Casiphia, that they should bring to us ministers for the house of our God. (8:17).

And since the gracious hand of our God was upon us, they brought us Sherebiah— a man of insight from the descendants of Mahli son of Levi, the son of Israel— along with his sons and brothers, 18 men; (8:18).
also Hashabiah, together with Jeshaiah, from the descendants of Merari, and his brothers and their sons, 20 men. (8:19).
They also brought 220 of the temple servants, all designated by name. David and the officials had appointed them to assist the Levites. (8:20).
And there by the Ahava Canal I proclaimed a fast, so that we might humble ourselves before our God and ask Him for a safe journey for us and our children, with all our possessions. (8:21).

For I was ashamed to ask the king for an escort of soldiers and horsemen to protect us from our enemies on the road, since we had told him, “The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him, but His great anger is against all who forsake Him.” (8:22).
So we fasted and petitioned our God about this, and He granted our request. (8:23).
Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests, together with Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers, (8:24).
and I weighed out to them the contribution of silver and gold and the articles that the king, his counselors, his leaders, and all the Israelites there had offered for the house of our God. (8:25).
I weighed out into their hands 650 talents of silver, articles of silver weighing 100 talents, 100 talents of gold, (8:26).
20 gold bowls valued at 1,000 darics, and two articles of fine polished bronze, as precious as gold. (8:27).
Then I told them, “You are holy to the LORD, and these articles are holy. The silver and gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers. (8:28).
Guard them carefully until you weigh them out in the chambers of the house of the LORD in Jerusalem before the leading priests, Levites, and heads of the Israelite families.” (8:29).
So the priests and Levites took charge of the silver and gold and sacred articles that had been weighed out to be taken to the house of our God in Jerusalem. (8:30).

On the twelfth day of the first month we set out from the Ahava Canal to go to Jerusalem, and the hand of our God was upon us to protect us from the hands of the enemies and bandits along the way. (8:31).
So we arrived at Jerusalem and rested there for three days. (8:32).

On the fourth day, in the house of our God, we weighed out the silver and gold and sacred articles into the hand of Meremoth son of Uriah, the priest. Eleazar son of Phinehas was with him, along with the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui. (8:33).
Everything was verified by number and weight, and the total weight was recorded at that time. (8:34).

Then the exiles who had returned from captivity sacrificed burnt offerings to the God of Israel: 12 bulls for all Israel, 96 rams, 77 lambs, and a sin offering of 12 male goats. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD. (8:35).
They also delivered the king’s edicts to the royal satraps and governors of the region west of the Euphrates, who proceeded to assist the people and the house of God. (8:36).
crossRefs: Ezra 7:11-26: The letter of Artaxerxes that authorises this caravan, funds it, and exempts the temple staff from tax.
Numbers 18:1-7: The Levites are joined to Aaron to guard the sanctuary, and only the priests may serve at the altar.
Numbers 4:4-15: The holy things are covered and carried on the shoulders of the Kohathites, who must not touch them.
Isaiah 52:11-12: Depart, touch no unclean thing, purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD.
Nehemiah 2:7-9: Nehemiah travels the same road to the same province with an escort of army officers and cavalry.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַנָּהָר הַבָּא אֶל־אַהֲוָא (hannahar habba el Ahava)
translationNotes.note: A watercourse in Babylonia, probably a canal, where Ezra held the caravan for three days to muster it and found there was not one Levite in the company (8:15). The site has never been identified. What matters in the narrative is that it was far enough from the city to camp and count.

They left on the twelfth day of the first month and reached Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month (7:9; 8:31), about four months in transit. Caravans did not cross the desert in a straight line; the road ran up the Euphrates and back down through Syria, roughly 900 miles, because water and towns lay that way. Ezra took women and children with him, which sets the pace.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַיִל וּפָרָשִׁים (chayil u-farashim, soldiers and horsemen)
translationNotes.note: Ezra says plainly he was ashamed to ask the king for troops after telling him God protects those who seek Him (8:22), so he proclaimed a fast at the river instead. He was carrying a fortune in unguarded metal through country where caravans were routinely robbed. Nehemiah, on the same road a few years later, accepted the cavalry (Nehemiah 2:9).

translationNotes.term: Weighed out and weighed back in
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וָאֶשְׁקֳלָה (va-eshqolah, and I weighed out)
translationNotes.note: Ezra weighs the silver, gold and vessels into the hands of twelve named priests, tells them they and the vessels are holy to the LORD, and has everything weighed again in the temple on arrival, with the totals written down (8:24-34). This is a chain of custody with named signatories at both ends. The charge in 8:28 is Isaiah 52:11 in substance: the men carrying the vessels of the LORD must themselves be set apart.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּכָּר (kikkar, talent) - אֲדַרְכֹּן (adarkon, daric)
translationNotes.note: Six hundred and fifty talents of silver, silver vessels worth a hundred talents, a hundred talents of gold, twenty gold bowls worth a thousand darics, and two vessels of fine bronze (8:26-27). At about 34 kilograms to the talent that is roughly 22 metric tons of silver and 3.4 metric tons of gold; the thousand darics of gold bowls weigh about 8.4 kilograms. This is a treasury convoy with no guards.

stories.keyTakeaway: Ezra assembles exiles returning from Babylon under King Artaxerxes, securing Levites and temple servants for the journey; after fasting and praying for protection, the group travels to Jerusalem with the donated silver, gold, and articles for the temple, which they deliver and weigh out before making burnt offerings.

headings.text: The Exiles Who Returned with Ezra

stories.title: 🙏 Ezra 9
summaryBullets: After these things had been accomplished, the leaders approached me and said, “The people of Israel, including the priests and Levites, have not kept themselves separate from the surrounding peoples whose abominations are like those of the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites. (9:1).

Indeed, the Israelites have taken some of their daughters as wives for themselves and their sons, so that the holy seed has been mixed with the people of the land. And the leaders and officials have taken the lead in this unfaithfulness!” (9:2).
When I heard this report, I tore my tunic and cloak, pulled out some hair from my head and beard, and sat down in horror. (9:3).
Then everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around me because of the unfaithfulness of the exiles, while I sat there in horror until the evening offering. (9:4).
At the evening offering, I got up from my humiliation with my tunic and cloak torn, and I fell on my knees, spread out my hands to the LORD my God, (9:5).
and said: “O my God, I am ashamed and embarrassed to lift up my face to You, my God, because our iniquities are higher than our heads, and our guilt has reached the heavens. (9:6).

From the days of our fathers to this day, our guilt has been great. Because of our iniquities, we and our kings and priests have been delivered into the hands of the kings of the earth and subjected to the sword and to captivity, to pillage and humiliation, as we are this day. (9:7).

But now, for a brief moment, grace has come from the LORD our God to preserve for us a remnant and to give us a stake in His holy place. Even in our bondage, our God has given us new life and light to our eyes. (9:8).

Though we are slaves, our God has not forsaken us in our bondage, but He has extended to us grace in the sight of the kings of Persia, giving us new life to rebuild the house of our God and repair its ruins, and giving us a wall of protection in Judah and Jerusalem. (9:9).
And now, our God, what can we say after this? For we have forsaken the commandments (9:10).

that You gave through Your servants the prophets, saying: ‘The land that you are entering to possess is a land polluted by the impurity of its peoples and the abominations with which they have filled it from end to end. (9:11).

Now, therefore, do not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters for your sons. Never seek their peace or prosperity, so that you may be strong and may eat the good things of the land, leaving it as an inheritance to your sons forever.’ (9:12).

After all that has come upon us because of our evil deeds and our great guilt (though You, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserve and have given us such a remnant as this), (9:13).
shall we again break Your commandments and intermarry with the peoples who commit these abominations? Would You not become so angry with us as to wipe us out, leaving no remnant or survivor? (9:14).
O LORD, God of Israel, You are righteous! For we remain this day as a remnant. Here we are before You in our guilt, though because of it no one can stand before You.” (9:15).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 7:1-4: Israel is not to intermarry with the nations of Canaan, because they will turn the sons away to serve other gods.
Deuteronomy 23:3-8: No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD; Egyptians and Edomites may in the third generation.
Exodus 34:12-16: Do not cut a covenant with the people of the land or take their daughters for your sons, or they will lead you after their gods.
Judges 3:5-7: Israel took their daughters and gave their own, and served the Baals and the Asherahs.
Daniel 9:4-19: A prayer from the exile that owns the nation's guilt and pleads God's own name, not Israel's merit.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַמֵּי הָאֲרָצוֹת (ammei ha-aratsot, the peoples of the lands)
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 lists Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians and Amorites. That combines two different laws: the Canaanite nations of Deuteronomy 7:1, whom Israel was to make no marriage with, and Ammon, Moab and Egypt, whom Deuteronomy 23:3-8 handles under a separate rule about entering the assembly. The report to Ezra is quoting law at him, and he answers it in 9:11-12 by quoting the prophets back.

translationNotes.term: Tearing the garment and pulling out hair
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָרַעְתִּי אֶת־בִּגְדִי וּמְעִילִי (qarati et bigdi u-me'ili)
translationNotes.note: Tearing the tunic and the outer cloak at the neck was the standard sign of grief and horror (Genesis 37:34; 2 Kings 19:1). Ezra goes further and pulls hair out of his own head and beard, which is not ordinary mourning; it is a public act of shame at something he holds himself answerable for. Nehemiah, facing the same problem later, pulled out other men's hair instead (Nehemiah 13:25).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִנְחַת הָעָרֶב (minchat ha-arev)
translationNotes.note: The second of the two daily burnt offerings commanded in Exodus 29:38-42, made in mid-afternoon, around what the New Testament calls the ninth hour. It was a fixed hour of public prayer at the temple, which is why Daniel 9:21 and Acts 3:1 date events by it. Ezra sits stunned from morning until that hour, then kneels.

translationNotes.term: A peg in His holy place
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָתֵד (yated, tent peg or wall spike)
translationNotes.note: In 9:8 Ezra thanks God for leaving a remnant and giving them 'a peg in His holy place'. A yated is the stake that holds a tent down in wind, or the spike driven into a wall to hang gear on. The picture is a small, fixed hold in a place you could otherwise be blown out of; Isaiah 22:23 uses the same image of a peg driven in a sure place.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָשִׁים נָכְרִיּוֹת (nashim nokhriyyot)
translationNotes.note: The word nokhri means foreign in the sense of belonging to another people and another god, and 9:1-2 states the problem as adopting 'their abominations'. Deuteronomy 7:4 gives the reason for the law in one line: they will turn your sons away from following Me. Scripture elsewhere records foreign women who joined Israel and its worship, Rahab of Jericho and Ruth the Moabitess, both of them in the ancestry of David.

stories.keyTakeaway: Ezra learns that Israelites have intermarried with neighboring peoples contrary to God's commands, tears his clothes in distress, and prays a confession acknowledging the people's unfaithfulness and begging God's mercy despite their deserved punishment.

stories.title: 🙏 Ezra 10
summaryBullets: While Ezra prayed and made this confession, weeping and falling facedown before the house of God, a very large assembly of Israelites — men, women, and children — gathered around him, and the people wept bitterly as well. (10:1).

Then Shecaniah son of Jehiel, an Elamite, said to Ezra: “We have been unfaithful to our God by marrying foreign women from the people of the land, yet in spite of this, there is hope for Israel. (10:2).

So now let us make a covenant before our God to send away all the foreign wives and their children, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the command of our God. Let it be done according to the Law. (10:3).
Get up, for this matter is your responsibility, and we will support you. Be strong and take action!” (10:4).
So Ezra got up and made the leading priests, Levites, and all Israel take an oath to do what had been said. And they took the oath. (10:5).

Then Ezra withdrew from before the house of God and walked to the chamber of Jehohanan son of Eliashib. And while he stayed there, he ate no food and drank no water, because he was mourning over the unfaithfulness of the exiles. (10:6).
And a proclamation was issued throughout Judah and Jerusalem that all the exiles should gather at Jerusalem. (10:7).
Whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property, according to the counsel of the leaders and elders, and would himself be expelled from the assembly of the exiles. (10:8).

So within the three days, all the men of Judah and Benjamin assembled in Jerusalem, and on the twentieth day of the ninth month, all the people sat in the square at the house of God, trembling regarding this matter and because of the heavy rain. (10:9).
Then Ezra the priest stood up and said to them, “You have been unfaithful by marrying foreign women, adding to the guilt of Israel. (10:10).
Now, therefore, make a confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers, and do His will. Separate yourselves from the people of the land and from your foreign wives.” (10:11).
And the whole assembly responded in a loud voice: “Truly we must do as you say! (10:12).
But there are many people here, and it is the rainy season. We are not able to stay out in the open. Nor is this the work of one or two days, for we have transgressed greatly in this matter. (10:13).

Let our leaders represent the whole assembly. Then let everyone in our towns who has married a foreign woman come at an appointed time, together with the elders and judges of each town, until the fierce anger of our God in this matter is turned away from us.” (10:14).
(Only Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah, supported by Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite, opposed this plan.) (10:15).

So the exiles did as proposed. Ezra the priest selected men who were family heads, each of them identified by name, to represent their families. On the first day of the tenth month they launched the investigation, (10:16).
and by the first day of the first month they had dealt with all the men who had married foreign women. (10:17).
Among the descendants of the priests who had married foreign women were found these descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak and his brothers: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah. (10:18).
They pledged to send their wives away, and for their guilt they presented a ram from the flock as a guilt offering. (10:19).
From the descendants of Immer: Hanani and Zebadiah. (10:20).
From the descendants of Harim: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah. (10:21).
From the descendants of Pashhur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah. (10:22).
Among the Levites: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (that is, Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer. (10:23).
From the singers: Eliashib. From the gatekeepers: Shallum, Telem, and Uri. (10:24).
And among the other Israelites, from the descendants of Parosh: Ramiah, Izziah, Malchijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Malchijah, and Benaiah. (10:25).
From the descendants of Elam: Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah. (10:26).
From the descendants of Zattu: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza. (10:27).
From the descendants of Bebai: Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai. (10:28).
From the descendants of Bani: Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth. (10:29).
From the descendants of Pahath-moab: Adna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh. (10:30).
From the descendants of Harim: Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, Shimeon, (10:31).
Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah. (10:32).
From the descendants of Hashum: Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei. (10:33).
From the descendants of Bani: Maadai, Amram, Uel, (10:34).
Benaiah, Bedeiah, Cheluhi, (10:35).
Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib, (10:36).
Mattaniah, Mattenai, and Jaasu. (10:37).
From the descendants of Binnui: Shimei, (10:38).
Shelemiah, Nathan, Adaiah, (10:39).
Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai, (10:40).
Azarel, Shelemiah, Shemariah, (10:41).
Shallum, Amariah, and Joseph. (10:42).
And from the descendants of Nebo: Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Jaddai, Joel, and Benaiah. (10:43).
All these men had married foreign women, and some of them had children by these wives. (10:44).
crossRefs: Nehemiah 13:23-27: Nehemiah confronts the same intermarriage a generation later and names Solomon as the warning.
Malachi 2:10-16: The prophet indicts marriage to the daughter of a foreign god and treachery against the wife of one's youth.
2 Chronicles 15:9-15: Judah gathers in a great assembly and binds itself by oath to seek the LORD.
Joshua 24:14-25: Israel at Shechem swears to put away the foreign gods their fathers served beyond the River.
Deuteronomy 24:1-4: The law of the certificate of divorce and the woman who leaves a man's house.

translationNotes.term: The ninth month, sitting in the rain
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַחֹדֶשׁ הַתְּשִׁיעִי (hachodesh hatteshi'i, the ninth month)
translationNotes.note: Kislev, mid-November to mid-December, is the start of the winter rains in Judah. The whole assembly sits in the open square in front of the temple, shaking from the rain and from the business at hand (10:9), and their own proposal in 10:13 is that the rains are heavy and this cannot be settled in a day or two. That is why the commission sat for three months instead.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִכְרֹת־בְּרִית (nikhrot berit, let us cut a covenant)
translationNotes.note: The man who stands up and proposes the covenant is Shecaniah son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam (10:2). A Jehiel of the sons of Elam appears on the final list of men who had married foreign wives (10:26). The proposal comes from inside the affected families, not from the officials.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הוֹצִיא (hotsi, to send out)
translationNotes.note: The verb used in 10:3 and 10:19 is the ordinary legal term for sending a wife out of the house, that is, divorce, which Deuteronomy 24:1 regulates with a written certificate. The text also records the dissent: four men are named as opposing the plan (10:15). Ezra reports both the decision and the objection without smoothing either one over.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָשָׁם (asham, guilt or reparation offering)
translationNotes.note: In 10:19 the priests who had married foreign wives pledge to put them away and bring a ram from the flock for their guilt. The asham of Leviticus 5:14-19 is the offering for a wrong that has to be made good, not merely confessed. It is the offering you bring when restitution is part of the remedy.

translationNotes.term: The commission that sat three months
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָאשֵׁי הָאָבוֹת (rashei ha-avot, heads of fathers' houses)
translationNotes.note: Case by case, with elders and judges from each town, from the first day of the tenth month to the first day of the first month (10:16-17). Nobody was expelled by a blanket ruling; each household was heard by name. The list that closes the book is the record of that inquiry, priests first, then Levites, singers and gatekeepers, then the laity by family.

stories.keyTakeaway: Ezra leads the exiles in a covenant to divorce their foreign wives; officials and judges investigate the cases over three months and produce a list of those who had married foreign women, including priests, Levites, and other Israelites.

intro:
Ezra was written by Ezra the priest and scribe himself, the same author who composed Chronicles, according to Jewish tradition (Talmud Baba Bathra 15a) and confirmed by the book's own first-person sections in chapters 7-10 (where the text shifts from "Ezra did this" to "I, Ezra"). The book reached its final form in post-exilic Jerusalem around 450-430 BC, shortly after the events of Ezra's reforms in 458-444 BC. Ezra was a priest of the line of Aaron through Phinehas (Ezra 7:1-5), a "skilled scribe in the Law of Moses" (Ezra 7:6), born and raised in Babylon during the exile, and sent to Jerusalem in 458 BC by the Persian king Artaxerxes I with royal authority to teach the Law, judge cases, and reorganize temple worship. He traveled from Babylon to Jerusalem at the head of a group of returning exiles in a journey of roughly four months, refusing a royal military escort and instead fasting for safe passage (Ezra 8:21-23). Jewish tradition holds that Ezra founded the Great Assembly (Knesset Gedolah), the body that helped fix the Hebrew canon and standardize liturgical practice. The events of the book cover roughly 538 to 444 BC; the first six chapters narrate the earlier return under Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest (538 BC) and the rebuilding of the temple completed in 516 BC, while the last four chapters cover Ezra's own arrival in 458 BC and the subsequent reforms. The historical setting is the Persian period under the Achaemenid Empire, with Yehud (the Persian province encompassing former Judah) administered from Jerusalem as a small satrapy. Persia's emperors during this span include Cyrus the Great (who issued the return decree in 539 BC), Cambyses II, Darius I (during whose reign the temple was completed), Xerxes I (Ahasuerus of Esther), and Artaxerxes I (Ezra's commissioning king). Egypt was a Persian satrapy under the 27th Dynasty; Greece was at the height of its Classical period (Pericles in Athens, the rise of philosophy under Socrates).

Ezra is the fifteenth book of the Christian Old Testament. In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah were originally counted as a single book within the Ketuvim (Writings); the Greek Septuagint translators distinguished them as Esdras B (Ezra) and a separate Esdras (Nehemiah), and the Latin Vulgate separated them into two distinct books, the arrangement inherited by English Bibles. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Ezra were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the Persian period or shortly after.
